# Synthetic anti-RNA antibody derivatives for RNA visualization in mammalian cells

**Authors:** Hasan Al Banna; Kimberley Berg; Tasnia Sadat; Naba Krishna Das; Roshan Paudel; Victoria D'Souza; Deepak Koirala

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of Maryland, Baltimore County, Baltimore, MD 21250, USA | Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA | Department of Computer Science, Morgan State University, Baltimore, MD 21251, USA

## Abstract

Although antibody derivatives, such as Fabs and scFvs, have revolutionized the cellular imaging, quantification and tracking of proteins, analogous tools and strategies are unavailable for cellular RNA visualization. Here, we developed four synthetic anti-RNA scFv (sarabody) probes and their green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusions and demonstrated their potential to visualize RNA in live mammalian cells. We expressed these sarabodies and sarabody–GFP modules, purified them as soluble proteins, characterized their binding interactions with their corresponding epitopes and finally employed two of the four modules, sara1-GFP and sara1c-GFP, to visualize a target messenger RNA in live U2OS cells. Our current RNA imaging strategy is analogous to the existing MCP-MS2 system for RNA visualization, but additionally, our approach provides robust flexibility for developing target RNA-specific imaging modules, as epitope-specific probes can be selected from a library generated by diversifying the sarabody complementarity determining regions. While we continue to optimize these probes, develop new probes for various target RNAs and incorporate other fluorescence proteins like mCherry and HaloTag, our groundwork results demonstrated that these first-of-a-kind immunofluorescent probes will have tremendous potential for tracking mature RNAs and may aid in visualizing and quantifying many cellular processes as well as examining the spatiotemporal dynamics of various RNAs.

## Introduction

RNA imaging in cells provides critical information about its dynamics, transport and localization, which is crucial for understanding gene expression and regulatory processes in normal and disease cellular conditions (1–3). A common strategy to visualize cellular RNAs has been to label the RNA with fluorescent probes, including incorporating fluorophores via chemical reactions or hybridization-based approaches and using genetically encoded fluorophore modules (1–3). While recent developments in bioorthogonal click chemistry approaches facilitated the direct labeling of RNA with the fluorophore-attached nucleobases (4), the fluorophore-labeled oligonucleotide probes offered more sensitive and sequence-specific methods, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization and molecular beacons (5,6). However, the challenges associated with the cellular delivery of the modified nucleobases or oligonucleotides with fluorophores and the perturbation of various cellular processes by these unnatural probes have been the limiting factors for the broader application of these approaches for live cell RNA imaging (3).

The genetically encodable fluorophore modules offer several advantages over the probes developed through chemical modifications for live cell RNA imaging. While several variants of the methodologies exist, cellular RNA imaging strategies using genetically encoded probes mainly involve two approaches. The first approach uses RNA aptamer tags that can fluoresce upon binding with fluorophore ligands. Various aptamers and fluorophore ligands have been developed and successfully applied to visualize RNA in bacteria and mammalian cells (7,8). Nevertheless, this approach requires tagging target RNA by the non-native RNA structure and efficient cellular intaking of the fluorophore. The cellular permeability of the fluorophores, proper folding of aptamer RNA in cells, non-compliance with cellular RNA degradation machinery and alteration of target RNA properties by the tag insertion are the significant concerns that have challenged robust applications of these fluorophore aptamer-based probes (9,7,10).

The other and most widely used approach to visualize RNA in cells is based on naturally occurring fluorescent protein probes. The module consists of an RNA-binding protein (RBP) probe that binds to a specific RNA motif incorporated as the tag within the RNA target and a fluorescent protein fused with the RBP probe that allows the visualization. Several protein-based RNA imaging modules have been developed through this approach using a combination of different fluorescent proteins and a limited set of related viral RBP probes such as MCP and PP7 (11–13). Among the RBP-based modules, the MCP-MS2 system so far has been the gold-standard method for cellular RNA visualization, and it has been used to visualize various steps of the messenger RNA (mRNA) life cycle (14–16). It uses a fluorescent protein such as green fluorescent protein (GFP) fused with MS2 bacteriophage coat protein (MCP), where the MCP probe recognizes the MS2 RNA hairpins inserted within the RNA target (17). The MCP binding site is known to form a stable RNA hairpin structure (18,19), and typically, at least 24 MS2 hairpins per target RNA are required for the optimal signal-to-noise ratios (14–16). While the MCP-MS2 system has been valuable in visualizing select RNAs, it has several drawbacks. The tight binding affinity of the MCP with MS2 hairpins has been shown to impair the mRNA degradation, leaving the MCP-MS2 hairpin complex products and making it difficult to distinguish the visualization of the intact or degraded mRNAs using this system (20–22). Some variants of the MS2 hairpins with tailored affinity to the MCP have been developed to facilitate the visualization of short-lived mRNAs (23). Each cellular RNA is different in its sequence and structure; therefore, a system that works for one specific RNA may not apply to another and depending on the nature of the cellular RNAs, insertion of the MS2 stem loops has been shown to induce severe effects on the localization, stability, and behavior of some RNA targets (20,21,24,25). Moreover, the orthogonal systems with multiple probe options are desirable for simultaneous visualization of multiple mRNAs in a single cell. Whereas a variety of natural and engineered fluorescent proteins with different spectral properties, such as GFP, mCherry and HaloTag, are available, the probes are limited to a few natural RBPs that are practically unmodifiable to integrate alternative epitopes. Therefore, developing alternative probes for cellular RNA visualization is highly valuable for advancing the RNA biology field.

Antibody derivatives such as Fabs and scFvs against peptides and proteins have revolutionized the imaging and quantification of proteins in vivo with single-molecule resolution, including the real-time tracking of translation steps, the observation of nascent polypeptides being translated, and even the monitoring of the post-translational modifications (15,26–32). Nevertheless, there is a lack of such an antibody-based toolbox and analogous strategies for RNA visualization in live cells. Here, we developed synthetic anti-RNA scFv (named sarabody) probes and their GFP fusions that have great potential to study RNA in vitro and in vivo. Our current RNA imaging strategy is analogous to the MCP-MS2 system; however, the probes are built uniquely from antibody derivatives (scFvs) that provide an alternative toolkit for live-cell RNA imaging with a robust platform for developing modifiable probe-epitope pairs. When expressed in cells with target RNAs, sarabody probes bind to the desired epitope tags inserted within the RNA targets, and the GFP fluorescence allows visual detection. However, unlike existing systems, such as MCP-MS2, the antibody-based probes offer great flexibility in developing various probe-epitope pairs with a broad range of binding affinities. The complementarity determining regions (CDRs) of the sarabody probe can be diversified to construct a library for selecting probes for the target-specific epitopes via in vitro methods like phage display selection (33–35). Our approach thus also allows the facile development of orthogonal probes to facilitate cellular imaging of more than one mRNA species in a single cell. While further investigation is needed to explore the full potential of our strategy, at this stage, it could be an excellent alternative to the MCP-MS2 system while expanding the repertoire of the cellular RNA visualization probes.

Notably, sarabodies can be developed to directly bind the structural features within the RNA target (36–38), which could, in principle, bypass the requirement for external insertion of the epitopes. Such flexibility would simplify the visualization of RNAs with repeats of the same structural features in the native sequence and structural contexts, such as Xist non-coding RNA that contains ∼8 repeats of the same hairpin structure (39). Moreover, while detecting a single-molecule fluorescence by conventional microscopy methods is challenging, with the advancement of microscopy and brighter fluorophores in the future, sarabody probes are readily amenable to visualize the single unmodified RNAs in living cells. Therefore, we anticipate that, like the protein visualization strategies, our sarabody approach will allow the tracking of mature RNAs and visualizing and quantifying the cotranscriptional folding and dynamics of nascent RNA (prokaryotes), conformational changes and spatiotemporal dynamics of RNA molecules in living cells.

We derived the sarabody probes from the existing anti-RNA Fabs called BL3-6 (40), HCV2 (38) and HCV3 (38). We used these Fabs as our model systems because they are structurally well-characterized, as they have been used previously as chaperones for RNA crystallization and structure determination (38,41–43). The transformation of these Fabs into the sarabodies involved two different strategies. The first strategy involved grafting all six CDRs of the Fabs into an existing scFv scaffold (HA-frankenbody) proven to fold and function appropriately in cells (32) such that the resulting chimeric scFvs acquire the epitope specificity of the grafted CDRs while retaining the stability and solubility from the scaffold. In the second strategy, the light-chain and heavy-chain variable domains of each Fab were connected directly via a standard linker (3 × GGGGS sequence) to transform the Fabs into the corresponding scFvs. We designed, expressed and purified multiple sarabodies as soluble proteins and characterized their binding with corresponding RNA epitopes using native gel electrophoresis and biolayer interferometry (BLI). For the proof-of-concept, we also developed sarabody–GFP modules for the four sarabodies. These sarabody–GFP modules also bind to their cognate RNA epitopes similar to the parent Fabs and the sarabodies alone, which thus allowed us to use these newly developed probes to visualize a target RNA in live mammalian cells. While we demonstrated that our probes work similarly to the MCP-MS2 system, our ongoing projects include the further optimization of these probes for various cell types, the development of new probes for various RNA targets and the incorporation of fluorescent proteins with different spectral properties, such as mCherry and HaloTag. Nevertheless, our results are promising and demonstrate that these first-of-a-kind anti-RNA immuno-fluorescent probes have tremendous potential for RNA visualization in living cells.

## Materials and methods

### Materials

The DNA and protein sequences of all recombinantly expressed sarabody and sarabody–GFP constructs used in this study have been provided in Supplementary Table S1.

### Sarabody expression and purification

The codon-optimized sequences encoding different sarabodies and sarabody–GFP fusions were cloned into a pET-22b(+) vector (GenScript, www.genscript.com). The expressed protein sequence contained a vector-encoded 6× His tag at the C-terminal for the subsequent purification. The expression plasmids were then transformed into BL21 (DE3) Escherichia coli, and the cells were cultured in a 2× yeast extract tryptone (YT) medium supplemented with 100 μg/ml carbenicillin at 37°C with 220 rpm shaking until the optical density (OD) of ∼0.6. The cells were then induced for protein expression by using isopropylthio-β-galactoside (IPTG) to the final concentration of 0.5 mM, grown for 8 h at 30°C, and harvested by centrifugation at 7500 × g. The cell pellet was then resuspended in a lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris HCl, pH 7.5, 300 mM NaCl and 5 mM imidazole and lysed using sonication (Qsonica700, Cole-Parmer). The lysate was centrifuged at 39000 × g at 4°C, and the supernatant was passed through a 0.45-µm filter. The clarified lysate was then applied to a HisTrap™ HP column (Cytiva), and the protein was eluted from the column with a buffer (50 mM Tris HCl, 300 mM NaCl and 250 mM imidazole, pH 7.5) after washing the column with 5 column volumes of the lysis buffer. The eluted fractions were collected, dialyzed against a phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) buffer (137 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM KCl, 10 mM Na2HPO4, 1.8 mM KH2PO4) and loaded into a HiTrapTM Protein L column (Cytiva). The eluted fractions from the Protein L column were purified further by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) (HiLoadTM 16/600 SuperdexTM 75 pg column, Cytiva) using the storing buffer [25 mM 4-(2-hydroxyethyl) piperazine-1-ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES), pH 7.9, 12.5 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 0.1 mM ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 1 mM 1,4-dithiothreitol (DTT), 5% glycerol]. The single-peak protein fractions were then pooled and concentrated using the Amicon centrifugal filters (molecular weight cut-off 10 kDa, Millipore Sigma), flash frozen with liquid N2 in small aliquots and stored at −80°C until used. The purification of the GFP-tagged sarabodies followed similar steps. However, the eluted fractions from the HisTrapTM HP columns were subjected to the SEC without passing through the Protein-L column. The small-scale SEC purification and analysis used a Superdex® 75 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva).

### Fab expression and purification

Fab BL3-6, HCV2 and HCV3 expression plasmids were a kind gift from Joseph Piccirilli, the University of Chicago. The Fab was purified according to the published protocols (36,40,44). Briefly, the plasmid was transformed into 55244 E. coli competent cells and streaked into a Luria-Bertani (LB) agar plate with 100 μg/ml of carbenicillin. Several colonies were selected to inoculate a 15 ml starter culture and grown at 30°C for 8 h. The starter culture was then used to inoculate 1 liter of 2× YT media, and cells were grown for 24 h at 30°C. For Fab overexpression, the cells were centrifuged at 22°C and 7500 × g for 10 min, resuspended in 1L phosphate-depleted media and grown for 24 h at 30°C. The cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4°C and 7500 × g for 10 min, resuspended in 1× PBS (pH 7.4) buffer with 0.01 mg/ml bovine pancreas DNase I (Sigma-Aldrich), and 0.5 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) and lysed by sonication (Qsonica, Cole-Parmer). The mixture was first centrifuged at 39000 × g, the clear lysate was filtered through a 0.45-µm filter (VWR), and the Fab was purified using the Bio-Rad NGC fast protein liquid chromatography system. First, the lysate was passed through a HiTrapTM Protein A column (Cytiva), and the captured Fab was eluted with 0.1 M acetic acid. The fractions were collected, diluted 10 times using 1× PBS (pH 7.4) buffer and loaded into a HiTrapTM Protein G column (Cytiva). The eluted Fab fractions from the Protein G column in 0.1 M glycine, pH 2.7, were collected, diluted 10 times with a 50 mM NaOAc, 50 mM NaCl, pH 5.5 buffer and loaded into a HiTrapTM Heparin column (Cytiva). Finally, the Fab fractions eluted from the Heparin column by the gradient elution using 50 mM NaOAc, 2 M NaCl and pH 5.5 buffer were collected, and buffer was exchanged three times with 1× PBS (pH 7.4) using 30 kDa cut-off Amicon column (Millipore Sigma). The concentrated Fab was collected, analyzed by 12% sodium dodecyl sulphate-polyacrylamide (SDS) gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and tested for RNase activity using the RNaseAlert kit (Ambion, www.thermofisher.com). Aliquots (∼300 μl) of purified Fab were stored at −80°C until further use.

### RNA synthesis and purification

RNA constructs for sarabody binding and in vitro characterization were synthesized by in vitro transcription. DNA template with a T7 promoter sequence for transcription reaction was produced by polymerase chain reaction amplification of single-stranded DNA purchased from Integrated DNA Technologies. The first two nucleotides of reverse primer were 2′-OMe modified to reduce the 3′-end heterogeneity of the transcript (45). RNA was transcribed for 3 h at 37°C in a transcription buffer (composition: 40 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 10 mM NaCl, 25 mM MgCl2, EDTA 0.1 mM), along with 10 mM DTT, 2 mM spermidine, 40 U/ml RNase inhibitor, 5 U/ml TIPPase, 5 mM of each nucleotide (ATP, CTP, GTP, UTP), 50 pmol/ml DNA template and 50 μg/ml homemade T7 RNA polymerase (46). The transcription reaction was quenched by adding 10 U/ml DNase I (Promega) and incubating at 37°C for 1 h. All RNA samples were purified by denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (dPAGE). The band was visualized by ultraviolet (UV) shadowing, excised from the gel and eluted overnight at 4°C in 10 mM Tris, pH 8.0, 1 mM EDTA and 300 mM NaCl. The eluted RNA buffer was exchanged with pure water three times using a 10 kDa cut-off Amicon column (Millipore Sigma). RNA was collected, aliquoted into 300 μl fractions and stored at −80°C until further use.

### Native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis

For native RNA binding assay, the RNA sample purified by dPAGE was refolded in a buffer containing 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 10 mM MgCl2, and 100 mM NaCl. First, the RNA was heated at 90°C for 1 min, and an appropriate volume of 10× refolding buffer was added, followed by incubation at 50°C for 10 min and then in ice for 5 min. The refolded RNA was then incubated with different equivalents of Fab, sarabody or the sarabody–GFP proteins for 30 min at room temperature. The protein–RNA complex samples were mixed with an appropriate volume of 6× native gel loading dye containing 30% glycerol, 0.1% each bromophenol blue and xylene cyanol. The RNA–protein complex samples, along with the control samples, were loaded onto 10% native polyacrylamide gels and run at 120 V in 0.5× TBE buffer pH 7.5 (50 mM Tris-base, 50 mM Boric acid and 1 mM EDTA, pH 7.5) at room temperature. The gels were stained with ethidium bromide and imaged using the Azure 200 gel documentation system (Azure Biosystems).

### AlphaFold2 prediction

The AlphaFold2 v2.3.3 was used to predict the 3D structures of the designed sarabodies. The amino acid sequences of all sarabodies were entered at once into the AlphaFold-2 provided by Google’s Colabnotebook (47). The multimer model was used for the prediction, and the maximum number of recycling was set to six. The models for analysis were selected based on the predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) score (48). The structures were viewed and analyzed in PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.0 Schrödinger, LLC).

### Imaging constructs design

The sara1 and sara1c protein sequences were codon optimized for mammalian expression, synthesized and cloned into the HA-frankenbody-GFP mammalian expression construct by GenScript. The HA-frankenbody-GFP/HaloTag plasmids were a gift from the Stasevich Lab. The reporter design was based on the spaghetti monster (sm)HA-KDM5B-MS2 plasmid (Addgene #81085), wherein the MS2 stem-loop array was exchanged for 24 copies of the sara1/sara1c stem-loops (a mixture of gAAACAc and gAGACCc). This sara1/sara1c epitope array was synthesized and cloned into the spaghetti monster HA-KDM5B-MS2 plasmid by GenScript.

### Cell culture and transient transfection

U2OS cells (ATCC #HTB-96) were grown in a 37°C, 5% CO2 incubator. The growth media was Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) (Thermo Fisher #11 965 118) + 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (Avantor #97068–086) + 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo Fisher #15 140 122). For imaging, 1.3e5 U2OS cells were seeded on a glass bottom 35-mm dish (Ibidi #81218–200) at least 16 h before transfection. To enhance adherence of cells, the dishes were pre-coated with fibronectin (Millipore Sigma, #F1141) diluted in water to a working concentration of 7.85 μg/ml for at least 30 min, followed by a treatment of undiluted poly-l-ornithine (Bio-Techne #3436–100-01) for at least 1 h. The transfection plasmids were produced with a transfection-grade endotoxin-free miniprep kit (Takara #740490.50). For each transfection, 1.5 μg of the reporter plasmid + 0.5 μg HA-frankenbody-HaloTag plasmid + 0.1 μg of sarabody–GFP plasmid was used. We noted that although the HA-frankenbody-HaloTag and sara1/1c-GFP constructs are highly similar, we achieved the best results by transfecting less sara1/1c-GFP plasmid relative to HA-frankenbody-HaloTag. The samples transfected with 0.5 μg instead of 0.1 μg of sara1/1c-GFP tended to exhibit excessive GFP aggregation that hindered imaging. Before transfection, the media was changed to OptiMEM (Thermo Fisher #31 985 070). FuGENE HD (Promega, catalog #E2311) was used according to manufacturer specifications. The media was exchanged for growth media 3 h after transfection and incubated for at least 12 h.

### Live cell imaging

Phenol red-free DMEM (Thermo Fisher #21063029) + 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS) + 1% (v/v) penicillin/streptomycin (complete phenol red-free DMEM) was prepared for imaging. Cells were stained with Janelia Fluor 646 HaloTag ligand to image the HA-frankenbody-HaloTag probe (Promega #GA1121). The ligand was resuspended in sterile DMSO (Millipore Sigma #D2650) at 100 μM, aliquoted and frozen. To stain the cells, 1 μl of 100 μM ligand was diluted in 1 ml complete phenol red DMEM for a final concentration of 100 nM, and then cells were incubated in the diluted HaloTag ligand for 20 min. Following staining, the cells were washed twice with 2 ml of complete phenol-red free DMEM and taken directly to spinning disk confocal imaging. The imaging chamber was kept at 37°C with 5% CO2. The microscope stand is the Nikon Ti2. The spinning disk manufacturer and model is Nikon Yokogawa CSU-W1 with a 50-µm pinhole size. The microscope was equipped with a Mad City Labs piezo stage. The laser lines used were 488 and 640, and the laser modulation and exposure time were 75% and 100 ms, respectively. The filter used for the 488 laser was 525/36 nm. The filter used for the 640 laser was 705/72 nm. An LP 561 camera splitter separated the 488 and 640 emission wavelengths. The objective is a Nikon PlanApo 60 × objective with a numerical aperture 1.42. An Optovar magnification changer was applied to enhance magnification 1.5 times. Nikon F immersion oil was used on the lens. The microscope was equipped with dual Photometrics Prime BSI sCMOS cameras, so the color acquisition was made simultaneously. The bit depth was set to 12 bits with CMS gain. The Z-step used was 0.2 µm. Images were taken without delay for 1 min. The images were acquired with Nikon Elements version 5.42.04, and further analysis was done with Fiji.

## Results and discussion

### Sarabody constructs design strategies

Our strategies to design RNA-binding sarabodies for this study are based on the three existing anti-RNA Fabs BL3-6 (40), HCV2 (38) and HCV3 (38). These Fabs were developed previously through phage display selections and have been used in chaperone-assisted RNA crystallography (38,41–43). The Fab BL3-6 was originally selected against a ligase ribozyme (36) but later shown to bind the portable hairpin-loop epitope sequences 5′gAAACAc and 5′gAGACCc (49), which has been used to tag various RNAs, enabling Fab–RNA complex formation and the subsequent crystallography of the resulting Fab–RNA complexes (41–43). Similarly, the Fabs HCV2 and HCV3 were selected against the hepatitis C virus internal ribosome entry site (IRES) and were used to crystallize the JIIIabc domain within the IRES (38). Based on the known high-resolution crystal structures, we used two strategies to transform these Fabs into their corresponding scFvs. Because this approach successfully developed the HA-frankenbody previously (32), in our first approach, we designed the chimeric sarabodies by replacing all six CDRs of the HA-frankenbody with the corresponding CDRs of the Fabs (Figure 1A). As this anti-HA-tag scFv was shown previously to fold and function in live cells (32), the resulting chimeric sarabodies were expected to acquire the RNA-binding specificity from the grafted CDRs while retaining the stability of the HA-frankenbody scaffold. We have designated these chimeric sarabodies as sara1c and sara2c, corresponding to the parent Fabs BL3-6 and HCV2. In the second approach (Figure 1B), we directly connected two variable domain chains of the Fab by a linker sequence (3 × GGGGS) used previously for developing the HA-frankenbody (32). We have designated the resulting sarabodies as sara1, sara2, and sara3, corresponding to the parent Fabs BL3-6, HCV2, and HCV3.

### Structural features of the sarabodies

After designing the five scFv constructs, we investigated whether our sarabody sequences fold as designed using a de novo structure prediction based on the AlphaFold2 version 2.2.3 (50). To compute the structural models, we input all sarabody sequences into the AlphaFold software using Google Colab notebook, selected the multimer model and set up the maximum recycling number to six for better accuracy of the predicted structures. The reported structures of the sarabodies represent the models with a predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) score of 90 or higher, indicating a high prediction accuracy (48). Interestingly, the predicted models of chimeric sara1c and sara2c were very similar (all atoms RMSD = 0.466 Å and 0.398 Å) to their parent scaffold of the frankenbody crystal structure (Figure 1C and D) reported previously (PDB ID: 5B3N) (51), suggesting that the grafting of RNA binding Fab CDRs did not influence the overall similar structure of the frankenbody (see Supplementary Figure S2 for the comparisons of the CDR regions). Notably, the reported crystal structure is the 15F11 scFv, which has an identical scaffold as the HA-frankenbody (32). Consistent with the high conservation of the antibody scaffold structures, the predicted structures of the sara1c and sara2c also superimposed well (all atoms RMSD = 0.691 Å and 0.899 Å) with the scFv portion of their parent Fab BL3-6 and HCV2 crystal structures (Figure 1E and F, and Supplementary Figure S2). Similarly, the AlphaFold predicted structures of the sara1, sara2 and sara3 were very similar to the corresponding regions in the crystal structures of their parent Fabs (RMSDs for superpositions of sara1 : BL3-6 = 0.464 Å, sara2 : HCV2 = 0.665 Å and sara3 : HCV3 = 0.445 Å), indicating that these sarabodies are likely to retain their parental structural features as designed (Figure 1G, H and I, respectively, and see Supplementary Figure S2 for the comparisons of the CDR regions).

### Cytoplasmic expression and purification of sarabodies

Following designing the sarabodies, we sought to express and purify them as soluble proteins. For expression, first, we prepared the expression plasmid for each sarabody based on the pET-22b(+) vector that encodes for a 6× His tag at the C-terminal of the protein (Supplementary Figure S3). The plasmids were then transformed into various commonly used E. coli host strains, such as BL21 (DE3), Rosetta 2 (DE3) and 55244, for the cytoplasmic expression of the sarabodies. Because our sarabodies have the potential to form internal disulfide bonds (based on the Fab structures), for comparison, we also used the Origami B strain, which is known to facilitate the cytoplasmic folding of proteins with disulfide bonds (52). Although the sequences and structural models of all sarabodies are similar, the chimeric sarabodies sara1c and sara2c did not express in all four E. coli strains. However, the expression trials with all strains successfully produced the other three sarabodies as soluble proteins (Supplementary Figure S4). Because BL21 (DE3) strains are frequently used in many laboratories for protein expressions, we used the BL21 (DE3) strain to produce higher quantities of these sarabodies. The purification of the sarabodies from the bacterial lysate was performed via standard chromatographic approaches using the Ni-NTA, protein L and size-exclusion columns (see the ‘Materials and methods’ section for details). Figure 2A and B show the representative SEC and SDS gel electrophoresis results for the purified scFvs, suggesting the expected size, solubility, and homogeneity of the expressed sarabodies (see Supplementary Figure S5 for details of the Ni-NTA and protein L chromatograms). Notably, unlike the Fabs, the presence of the DTT did not change the SDS gel mobility of the sarabody bands (Figure 2B), suggesting that these proteins have no interchain disulfide bonds, consistent with a robust cytoplasmic expression of these sarabodies as soluble proteins even in the BL21 (DE3) strain.

### Binding of sarabodies with their cognate RNAs

After successfully expressing and purifying the sarabodies sara1, sara2 and sara3, we performed the binding studies with RNA constructs containing their cognate epitopes. For this, we prepared a CL RNA with the 5′GAAACAC3′ tag and the JIIIabc RNA construct (Supplementary Figure S6) such that the CL construct is expected to bind sara1 and the JIIIabc to sara2 and sara3. Because the crystal structures of the Fab–RNA complexes for these RNAs have been determined (38,42), they served as the ideal RNA constructs for testing the binding of these sarabodies. As shown by our native gel electrophoresis assays, all three sarabodies bound to their respective cognate RNAs as their corresponding Fabs (Figure 2C), consistent with high structural similarity between the sarabody models and parent Fab crystal structures. Notably, a single C to G mutation within the sara1 epitope (i.e. mutation of 5′gAAACAc to 5′gAAAGAc) abolished the sara1 binding to the target RNA (Supplementary Figure S7), illustrating the high specificity of the sarabody probes to their targets. Such high specificity of the sara1 is consistent with the enrichment of a consensus 5′gNGACCc hairpin loop sequence from a 40-nt randomized library of RNAs in an in vitro selection process with the Fab BL3-6 (49). During native gel electrophoresis assays, we often observed two bands for the sarabody–RNA complexes, with the upper complex band migrating slightly slower and the lower complex band migrating much faster compared to the corresponding Fab–RNA complexes (molecular weight, MW of Fab is ∼48 kDa and sarabody is ∼28 kDa), indicating that our sarabodies may form chain-swapped dimers (sarabody dimer MW ∼56 kDa) in the solution (Supplementary Figure S8). Nevertheless, although the ratio of monomeric and dimeric forms varied among the purification batches, these monomeric and dimeric forms were separable by SEC (Supplementary Figure S8). Accordingly, the subsequent binding tests with their cognate RNA constructs using gel electrophoresis showed sarabody–RNA complexes that were consistent with the monomeric and dimeric forms of the sarabodies.

Next, to quantitatively measure the sarabody–RNA binding interactions, we performed the BLI measurements. For this, the 6xHis-tagged sarabody was immobilized into an anti-His-tag biosensor, which was then dipped into the RNA solution to measure the time-dependent interference response caused by the RNA binding with the immobilized sarabody (see the ‘Materials and methods’ section for details). These measurements thus provided both kinetics and apparent steady-state binding affinities for the RNA–sarabody interactions. The kinetics measurements (Supplementary Figure S1) showed that the sara1 binds to the CL RNA with an association (kon) and dissociation (koff) rate constants 6.4 × 105 ± 8.4 × 103 M−1 s−1 and 7.7 × 10−3 ± 3.4 × 10−5 s−1, respectively. Similarly, the binding of sara2 (kon = 2.2 × 105 ± 3.3 × 103 M−1 s−1 and koff = 2.0 × 10−2 ± 8.8 × 10−5 s−1) and sara3 (kon = 2.3 × 105 ± 6.0 × 103 M−1 s−1 and koff = 2.0 × 10−2 ± 1.6 × 10−4 s−1) with the JIIIabc RNA showed a similar fast association and slow dissociation kinetics (Supplementary Figure S1), indicating that our sarabody probes are amenable to visualize several dynamic events that occur during RNA synthesis and folding in cells.

The kinetically measured binding affinities (Kd = 12.1 ± 0.2 nM, 90.9 ± 1.4 nM, and 91.3 ± 2.5 nM for the binding of sara1, sara2, and sara3 with their cognate RNAs, respectively) were similar within the same orders of magnitude to the apparent dissociation constant (Kd) measured from the RNA concentration-dependent responses (Figures 2C–E). The steady-state Kd for the binding of sara1 with the CL RNA (Figure 2F) was 154 ± 28 nM, similar to its parent Fab BL3-6 binding with the RNAs containing the 5′GAAACAC3′ tag (40). Similarly, the sara2 (Figure 2G) and sara3 (Figure 2H) bound to the JIIIabc (apparent Kds= 38 ± 23 nM and 361 ± 84 nM, respectively), consistent with their parent Fab HCV2 and HCV3 binding with the same JIIIabc RNA (38). The binding affinities of the sarabodies are similar to those of their parent Fabs, suggesting that they retain the folding and CDR structures of parent Fabs, which are consistent with their AlphaFold-predicted structures. Notably, the binding interface area (990 Å2) (18) for the MCP-MS2 hairpin binding is similar to that for the sara1, sara2 and sara3 (1102 Å2, 635 Å2 and 936 Å2, respectively), which is consistent with the similar nanomolar affinity of the MCP-MS2 hairpin binding (Kd ∼5 nM) (53,54) compared to that of our sarabody binding with their cognate RNAs. However, the sarabody binding to their cognate RNAs seems relatively weaker compared to that of MCP-MS2 binding, indicating that the sarabody probe-epitope complexes may be less prone to interfere with the mRNA degradation process as observed for the MCP-MS2 systems (20–23). These results are also consistent with the kinetic measurements of sarabody binding to their cognate RNAs (sara1 kon = 6.4 × 105 M−1 s−1 and koff = 7.7 × 10−3 s−1) and MCP binding with the MS2 hairpin (kon = 1.7 × 106 M−1 s−1, koff = 7.7 × 10−3 s−1) (53,54), suggesting that the sarabody probe-interactions are kinetically similarly stable to the MCP-MS2 system and will be applicable to visualize both the short and long-lived RNAs.

### Binding characterization of the sarabody–GFP fusions

After characterizing the binding of sarabodies with their cognate RNAs, we tagged each sarabody probe at the C-terminus with the same GFP sequence used in the HA-frankenbody (see Supplementary Table S1 for the sequences). The expression plasmids for each sarabody were based on the pET-22b(+) vector that encodes for a 6× His tag at the C-terminal of the sarabody–GFP fusion protein (Figure 3A). The plasmids were then transformed into the BL21 (DE3) E. coli strain for the cytoplasmic expression of the sarabody–GFP proteins. After the expression, the proteins from the bacterial lysate were purified via standard chromatographic approaches using the Ni-NTA and size-exclusion columns. All sarabody–GFP proteins were visibly green and showed the expected size band (∼56 kDa) in the SDS gel-electrophoresis after purification, suggesting a robust expression of these proteins in E. coli, and the scFv and GFP domains in the fusion protein were folded independently and adequately (Figure 3B and C). To demonstrate the binding of these fusion proteins with the cognate RNAs of the corresponding sarabody probes, we performed native gel electrophoresis with the same CL and the JIIIabc RNA constructs. As shown by our native gel electrophoresis assays, all three sarabody–GFP probes bound to their respective cognate RNAs as their corresponding sarabodies only (Figures 3C–E and Supplementary Figure S9), suggesting that the sarabody probe and the GFP domains fold independently. The migrations of the protein–RNA complex bands in the gel electrophoresis were slightly slower than the corresponding Fab–RNA complexes (Fab MW ∼48 kDa), consistent with the expected size of the sarabody–GFP fusion protein (MW ∼56 kDa). Notably, we observed multiple bands for the protein–RNA complexes also with the sarabody–GFP fusions, which may be due to the propensity of these proteins to dimerize through the sarabody probes and conformational heterogeneity because of the flexible linker between the probe and the GFP. We also noticed that some higher-order RNA–protein complexes or aggregates were stuck in gel wells (Figure 3D–F), explaining the somewhat lower binding affinity of the sarabody–GFP fusions than the corresponding sarabodies alone (Figures 2C–E).

### Visualization of a target RNA in live cells using sarabody probes

To demonstrate the feasibility of our sarabody probes for imaging RNAs in mammalian cells, we performed nascent chain tracking experiments (16) in live U2OS cells. Because the parent Fabs of sara2 and sara3 (HCV2 and HCV3, respectively) recognize a complicated tertiary interaction within the JIIIabc RNA (Supplementary Figure S6) (38), making it challenging to tag the target RNA with this relatively large epitope, we pursued RNA imaging studies with a relatively small and simple hairpin-loop epitope of the sara1 or sara1c. Though we completed in vitro binding studies with sara1 and not sara1c, due to the lack of expression of sara1c in bacteria, we tested the live cell microscopy performance of both probes. As explained previously, sara1c retains the HA-frankenbody scaffold, which is known to fold efficiently and bind its target well in mammalian cells (32). Therefore, we anticipated that sara1c may perform better as a genetically encoded immuno-fluorescent tag than sara1.

First, we placed the sara1 and sara1c GFP fusion protein sequences in a mammalian expression vector (sara1-GFP and sara1c-GFP). Second, we modified the smHA-KDM5B-MS2 reporter mRNA construct reported previously (32) by replacing the MS2 hairpin loops within the 3′ UTR of the construct with 24 copies of a mixture of 5′ gAAACAc or 5′ gAGACCc hairpin loops. This Sara1/1c Epitope-Rich reporter construct (smHA-KDM5B-SER) codes for the 10 copies of HA epitopes (referred to as spaghetti monster HA or smHA) fused to the large nuclear protein KDM5B (Figure 4A). The sarabody and HA-frankenbody-HaloTag probes are thus expected to allow for the visualization of individual mRNA transcripts and the nascent translating smHA-KDM5B protein, respectively (Figure 4A). The binding of both probes within the context of the single target mRNA transcript thus provides co-localized signals, demonstrating the ability of sarabody probes to bind actively translating mRNAs. To validate the efficacy of the sarabody probes for RNA imaging, U2OS cells were transiently transfected with the three plasmids encoding sara1-GFP or sara1c-GFP, smHA-KDM5B-SER, and HA-frankenbody-HaloTag for live-cell imaging experiments.

Excitingly, we observed discrete puncta from both sara1-GFP and sara1c-GFP signals, indicating that the probes bound to their target epitopes as expected (Figure 4B and C). Moreover, the puncta from the sarabody–GFP and the HA-frankenbody signals were colocalized, meaning that the observed GFP signals were due to specific RNA labeling rather than sarabody aggregation or non-specific binding (Figure 4B and C). However, we noted that the samples transfected with sara1c-GFP had a higher proportion of cells with colocalizing puncta, and the sara1-GFP puncta photobleached more quickly than sara1c-GFP puncta (Figure 4D and E). These results indicate that sara1c probes likely benefit from the stability of the frankenbody scaffold for folding in cells. While the HA-frankenbody-HaloTag and sara1c-GFP constructs are sequence-wise and structurally identical except for their CDRs, we achieved the best results transfecting only with one-fifth of the sara1c-GFP plasmid relative to the HA-frankenbody-HaloTag plasmid. This indicates that the sarabody–GFP mRNAs or corresponding proteins perhaps have a comparatively more robust expression or greater stability.

Notably, the colocalization of translation and RNA puncta persisted over time, suggesting that the sarabody probes bound their epitope with high affinity and formed stable sarabody–RNA complexes in cells (Figure 4D and E), which is consistent with our in vitro binding studies. We could also identify non-translating mRNA puncta (Figure 4E), supporting the feasibility of sarabodies for visualizing both actively translating and non-translating mRNAs. As sara1c performed better compared to sara1, we further tested its specificity using a control reporter construct (smHA-KDM5B-control) that contained the 24 copies of unrelated hairpin loops containing the 5′ CAAUGCAUAGGCG sequence instead of the sara1 or sara1c epitopes (Figure 5A). Consistent with our in vitro binding studies (Supplementary Figure S6), transfection of the cells with the smHA-KDM5B-control instead of the smHA-KDM5B-SER construct along with the sara1c-GFP probe mainly yielded the HaloTag puncta, underscoring the high specificity of sara1c probes to recognize their target epitopes in the milieu of cellular RNAs (Figure 5B and C). Some GFP puncta were also observed, but they appeared at a similar background level as in cells transfected only with sara1c-GFP in the absence of any reporter mRNA (Supplementary Figure S10), suggesting that these likely represent the free-floating aggregated sara1c-GFP. Notably, we observed that nearly all puncta from the GFP and HaloTag fluorescence were co-localized for the smHA-KDM5B-SER reporter compared to no colocalization at all for the smHA-KDM5B-control (Figure 5D), supporting the fact that these signals correspond to the same target mRNA transcript, resulting from specific binding of sara1c probe to its tagged epitopes. While the expansion of these sarabody probes to incorporate other fluorescent tags (such as mCherry and HaloTag) and the development of RNA target-specific sarabodies are underway, our initial studies have demonstrated that sarabody probes are a worthy addition to the RNA visualization toolkit with the potential to open a new avenue in the live cell RNA imaging field.

## Conclusions and future perspectives

Despite several limitations, MCP-MS2 and a few closely related modules are the only live cell RNA visualization options among various genetically encodable systems. Here, we presented a proof-of-concept principle for developing an alternative toolkit for RNA imaging in live mammalian cells. We created four sarabody probes and their GFP fusions from the existing anti-RNA Fabs. We expressed and purified these proteins and characterized their binding with the corresponding cognate RNAs using native gel electrophoresis and BLI measurements and revealed that the sarabody probes recognize their targets with comparable affinity and rate as the MCP-MS2 system. While it warrants further comparative investigations with different RNA targets, our current sarabody system is analogous to the MCP-MS2 system. It could be used alternatively for RNAs where the MCP-MS2 system malfunctions and vice versa. Nevertheless, our approach toward developing the first-of-a-kind immuno-fluorescent probes offers flexibility to generate various probe-epitope pairs. Given the availability of several other anti-RNA Fabs (55), this approach can be used to create target RNA-tailored probes to increase the number of shots on goal. Moreover, with the future advancement of imaging technology and brighter fluorophores, our sarabody probes will be readily amenable to visualize untagged RNA molecules in live mammalian cells as developing the target-specific sarabody probes can be easily achieved through methods such as phage display selection. While we continue our studies toward improving these sarabody probes for robustness and multi-color imaging and developing RNA-target-specific probes in the future, our results reported here have already demonstrated the tremendous potential of anti-RNA antibody-based fluorescent probes for RNA visualization in live mammalian cells.

# Common light chain chickens produce human antibodies of high affinity and broad epitope coverage for the engineering of bispecifics

**Authors:** Kathryn H Ching; Kimberley Berg; Kevin Reynolds; Darlene Pedersen; Alba Macias; Yasmina N Abdiche; William D Harriman; Philip A Leighton

## Abstract

Bispecific antibodies are an important and growing segment in antibody therapeutics, particularly in the immuno-oncology space. Manufacturing of a bispecific antibody with two different heavy chains is greatly simplified if the light chains can be the same for both arms of the antibody. Here, we introduce a strain of common light chain chickens, called OmniClic®, that produces antibody repertoires largely devoid of light chain diversity. The antibody repertoire in these chickens is composed of diverse human heavy chain variable regions capable of high-affinity antigen-specific binding and broad epitope diversity when paired with the germline human kappa light chain. OmniClic birds can be used in immunization campaigns for discovery of human heavy chains to different targets. Subsequent pairing of the heavy chain with a germline human kappa light chain serves to facilitate bispecific antibody production by increasing the efficiency of correct pairing.

KEYWORDS: Bispecific, common light chain, transgenic chicken, human antibodies, antibody engineering

## Introduction

Bispecific antibodies (bsAbs) comprise a diverse collection of novel molecules in various formats and configurations designed to bind two distinct epitopes or targets at the same time. The pipeline of bsAbs in pharmaceutical development is quite large and diverse, with goals such as retargeting T effector cells to tumor cells, chaperoning proteins across the blood-brain barrier, anti-inflammatory effects, and increasing avidity by binding multiple epitopes on the same cell.1 In the case of retargeting of T cells to tumor cells, one arm of the bsAb is often specific for the CD3 delta or epsilon chains of the T cell receptor complex, and the other arm specific for a receptor on the tumor cells. To date, three bsAbs have been granted marketing approvals,2 although currently only two are on the market (blinatumomab (Blincyto®), for acute B-cell lymphoblastic leukemia, and emicizumab (Hemlibra®), for treating hemophilia A). With over 85 potential bsAbs in clinical development, this number is likely to rise.1

Using the modular domain structure of immunoglobulins, bispecific molecules have been formatted in myriad creative ways.3,4 These formats can be roughly divided into those that include the Fc domain and those that do not. Of those that include the Fc, some maintain an IgG-like structure that is similar to native IgG, whereas others take more creative structures not seen in nature such as multiple binding domains in tandem. Conforming to a more native IgG-like format offers advantages in patients, such as binding to FcRn and longer serum half-life, and potentially desired effector functions mediated by the intact Fc. More unusual formats may suffer from aggregation, longer development lead times, and require further engineering,5–7 whereas IgG-like formats are well-studied and have a long history in patients. However, bsAbs with an IgG-like format pose their own engineering challenges for manufacturing.2,3 Normal antibodies consist of a homodimer of a heavy-light chain pair, forming the two arms that both have the same antigen-binding site. In contrast, a bispecific antibody in IgG-like format must be a heterodimer with two distinct arms targeting the two distinct epitopes. If two different heavy chains and two different light chains were to be expressed in the same cell, then the various chains could assemble in 10 different combinations, only one of which would be the desired bispecific configuration.8 This challenging expression problem can be separated into the heavy chain pairing problem, in which the goal is an obligate heavy chain heterodimer with no homodimerization, and the light chain pairing problem, in which the correct light chain must pair with the correct heavy chain. By using two heavy chains that can pair with a common light chain, one of these two problems is solved, leaving only the heavy chain pairing problem. Various strategies at promoting heterodimerization or purifying heterodimers of the Fc domains of heavy chains have been developed.9–11 The common light chain strategy is most useful in IgG and IgG-like formats and eliminates a substantial hurdle in bispecific antibody production.

Discovery of heavy chains that can pair with a common light chain has been pursued either in display systems12–15 or in transgenic rodents.16–18 Conserved human targets may not be amenable to antibody discovery in rodent platforms due to the high degree of sequence homology, which can result in low immunogenicity. For targeting such antigens, chickens represent an evolutionarily divergent host in which most human proteins will induce a robust immune response, enabling antibody discovery when campaigns in rodents have failed.19–23 The chicken also readily produces antibodies that are cross-reactive to the mouse ortholog of the human target, obviating the need to identify surrogate antibodies for pre-clinical studies. As with campaigns for monospecific antibodies, bispecific antibody campaigns can benefit from the ability to identify mouse cross-reactive antibodies.24 In addition, as described below, the mechanisms of antibody generation in the chicken are uniquely suited to the engineering of a common light chain transgenic animal.

In chickens, development of the antibody repertoire is initiated when V(D)J recombination leads to expression of the functional B cell receptor on the surface of early B cells.25 However, unlike in mammals, very little diversity is produced at the recombination step. Chickens contain only a single functional V gene and a single J gene at the heavy and light chain loci,26,27 and the heavy chain contains a cluster of D segments that are highly related to each other.28 No terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase activity is present in chicken B cells, so no N addition can occur.29 Recombination thus produces essentially the same clonotype in every B cell, with the same V framework and nearly the same complementarity-determining regions (CDRs). As soon as recombination has produced a functional receptor, variable region sequences begin to mutate by the process of gene conversion, which leads to a highly diverse repertoire. Gene conversion incorporates sequences from an array of upstream pseudogenes in a homologous recombination-based process, leading to changes in the functional V. Multiple rounds of overlapping gene conversion occur from different pseudogenes, and indels can also be incorporated. In wild-type chickens, the light chain contains 25 pseudogenes and the heavy chain about 80 pseudogenes (the international ImMunoGeneTics information system, IMGT30). Pseudogene sequences contain diversity mainly in the CDRs, while the sequence of the VL/VH frameworks is largely maintained. However, in addition to gene conversion, random somatic hypermutation can also occur and adds to the sequence diversity in the repertoire.31

We have engineered chickens to express human V region antibodies (OmniChickens®).20,32 The constructs in these birds are designed with human pseudogenes containing diverse CDRs, to produce large repertoires of human sequences in the B cell population of these birds.20,33,34 Here, we pursued the opposite goal, at least for the light chain: a chicken with a non-mutating, common light chain that can pair with any heavy chain in the bird, for discovery of antibodies that can be developed into bispecifics. To design a light chain transgene in the chicken that does not produce a diverse sequence repertoire, we took advantage of gene conversion, but instead of inserting diverse pseudogenes, we inserted an array of identical pseudogenes to the functional human VK3-15/JK1 gene. The process of gene conversion and single framework architecture in the chicken is perfectly suited to this type of active suppression of antibody diversity, as compared to the typical mammalian locus with its multiple V genes that undergo recombination. In this common light chain chicken (called OmniClic®), not only will gene conversion not provide sequence diversity, it is designed to actively “cleanse” any mutations that may arise by random somatic hypermutation by reverting them to the wild-type sequence. Since we are taking advantage of the normal gene conversion process used by the chicken B cell, it is not necessary to make any other genetic or physiological changes to developing B cells, and diversity generation in the heavy chains should be unimpeded or possibly even encouraged given the lack of diversity in the light chain.

Here we show that the OmniClic chicken produces minimally mutated light chains. Despite the lack of light chain diversity, OmniClic raises robust immune responses upon immunization and produces high-affinity antibodies with diverse human heavy chains. Comparison to normal OmniChickens expressing diverse human heavy/light pairs shows that epitope binning and affinity are essentially normal when diversity is restricted to the heavy chain. The OmniClic platform can be used for antibody discovery of heavy chain sequences to be used with the germline VK3-15 light chain for bispecific applications.

## Results

### Generation of OmniClic birds

We set out to design a transgene construct that would express a human variable region light chain in chicken B cells that would remain unmutated, yet pair with diversified heavy chains to produce antibodies with high affinity and broad epitope coverage. This common light chain bird we call OmniClic, to distinguish it from our “standard” OmniChicken birds, which produce diverse repertoires in both light and heavy chains through gene conversion by upstream human-based pseudogenes. In OmniChickens, gene conversion events in the mature repertoire can be attributed to specific pseudogenes, showing that the pseudogenes are participating in gene conversion, even though most CDR sequences in mature antibodies are highly mutated and cannot be ascribed to identifiable gene conversion.20 To design OmniClic, we reasoned that an array of upstream pseudogenes identical to the germline functional V region could use the mechanisms of gene conversion to the opposite effect, i.e., to revert any mutations that might occur randomly by non-templated somatic hypermutation back to the germline sequence. This strategy effectively uses gene conversion to maintain the germline sequence, rather than producing a diverse repertoire of mutations. By using a pre-rearranged light chain and full-length reverting pseudogenes, we include all three CDRs in the reversion strategy. The enzymatic machinery for generating sequence diversity in immunoglobulins is conserved in chickens35,36 and depends on an initiating lesion by the activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) enzyme, leading to somatic hypermutation, gene conversion, or class switch recombination.37–39 These AID-based mechanisms remain intact in OmniClic, which is crucial because they are necessary to produce a diverse heavy chain repertoire and are also necessary for the reverting gene conversion strategy in the light chain.

The common light chain construct (CmLC1, Figure 1) in OmniClic is inserted in the chicken light chain locus, as are all the human light chain transgenes in OmniChicken, thereby utilizing the endogenous transcriptional regulatory elements and non-translated regions for optimal lineage-specific expression. This location also ensures that gene conversion in the B cell lineage will be focused on the light chain transgene.40,41 The variable region is a pre-rearranged VK3-15/JK1 region made by joining the germline gene segments together, with no chewing back of the ends. This rearranged sequence is expressed in humans, as it is found in the National Center for Biotechnology Information’s Expressed Sequence Tags database. The V region splices to the chicken CL constant region, producing a chimeric light chain. In the OmniClic locus, the chicken VL pseudogenes remain upstream of the human pseudogenes (Figure 1).

In OmniClic chickens, the CmLC1 light chain can be paired with either of the two human heavy chain transgenes that we use in OmniChicken lines, SynVH-C (pre-rearranged VH3-23/JH4) and SynVH-SD (rearranging VH3-23/Ds/JH6). In OmniChicken lines, these heavy chains are paired with the human V-kappa transgene (SynVK-CK; pre-rearranged VK3-15/JK4),20 or a human V-lambda transgene (SynVL-E-CL; VL1-44/JL3).32 The heavy chains are designed in a similar fashion to the light chains, each with a single functional human variable region, an array of upstream human pseudogenes for gene conversion, and splicing to the chicken constant regions for efficient engagement of Fc receptors and B cell receptor complexes in the bird. Chickens contain one light chain and one heavy chain. The human heavy and light transgenes are inserted at the endogenous heavy or light chain loci, and the other allele at each locus in the birds is a knockout (KO), so the only functional allele is the human transgene.26,27,42,43

### B cell development in OmniClic birds

OmniClic birds were evaluated for B cell development (Fig. S1). Peripheral blood lymphocytes were stained with antibodies to the chicken B cell marker Bu-1, surface IgM, IgL, T cell markers, and human VK3-15/VH3-23. Normal proportions of B cells were observed in OmniClic, and expression of human VK3-15/VH3-23 was detected. Since the constant regions of both the light and heavy chains are chicken, we can detect surface or plasma Ig using anti-chicken reagents and directly compare our transgenic birds to wild-type birds. Titers of total IgY levels in plasma were assessed and compared to wild-type chickens and the kappa and lambda OmniChicken strains (Fig. S2). The OmniClic chickens contained plasma IgY levels comparable to those in the V-lambda OmniChickens, which is about twofold below the wild-type level (Fig. S2). In contrast, V-kappa OmniChickens with the SynVK-CK construct express levels that are at least 10-fold lower than wild-type (Fig. S2).20 The fact that the CmLC1 construct expresses a higher level of serum Ig than the SynVK-CK construct, even though both contain human V-kappa, may stem from sequence differences in the contact residues of the V and C domains in these chimeric proteins. Based on structural modeling, the V and C domains make contacts at their interface, and the residue in the framework region (FR)4-CL junction is predicted to have contacts with the CL domain (Fig. S3). This residue is in a connecting loop between the domains, and its codon is split between the V exon and the C exon. This loop residue is Gly in CmLC1 and wild-type chicken light chain, but in SynVK-CK and wild-type human kappa it is Arg. The large, charged side chain of Arg in this position could hamper the ability of the human V region to fold efficiently with the chicken C region in SynVK-CK. There are a few other differences in FR1 and in the germline CDRs between CmLC1 and SynVK-CK, but they are not predicted to have an effect on the V-C interaction. The OmniChicken V-lambda construct is fully human (not chimeric), and therefore should have no inter-domain folding issues. Thus, the junction region between FR4 and the CL appears to be important for the efficient expression of a chimeric light chain with human VK and chicken CL.

### Immunization of OmniClic birds and evaluation of heavy and light chain repertoires produced

Birds were immunized with human progranulin protein (PGRN), a modular protein that we have used for comparison of immune responses across various genotypes of OmniChickens and wild-type chickens.19,20,32 PGRN is composed of 7.5 domains that can be used for identifying epitope binning patterns in a cohort of antibodies. Six OmniClic birds were immunized with human PGRN, three with the SynVH-C heavy chain and three with the SynVH-SD heavy chain, on a two-week interval of intramuscular boosts, with serum titers determined on the in-between weeks.20 High titers were obtained after the first boost (Fig. S4) and were comparable to those observed in OmniChickens.20 After reaching a sufficient titer, spleen lymphocytes were harvested and cryopreserved for either bulk sequence analysis or monoclonal antibody (mAb) recovery.

To assess overall levels of diversity in the antibody repertoire, next-generation sequencing (NGS) of CmLC and VH amplicons was performed on the six spleen samples from PGRN-immunized OmniClic birds and compared to similar data from normal OmniChickens also immunized with PGRN (heavy chains reported in Leighton et al.34). The regular OmniChickens served as a control for the level of diversity to be expected in light chains, as they were immunized with the same immunogen and the sequencing was performed the same way. In addition, the heavy chain transgenes are the same in all of the birds, which allowed us to compare the heavy chain repertoires produced when paired with either the common light chain or a mutating light chain. Primers for amplification of the V regions were chosen in the 5ʹ UTR and either the JK (for light chain) or IgY constant region (for heavy chain), to specifically analyze class-switched heavy chain sequences. Because there is only one functional framework (germline gene) for light chain and one for heavy chain, only a single primer pair is necessary to capture all of the expressed light (or heavy) variable region sequences, which obviates the risk of amplification bias from mixtures of V-family primers that are required to amplify the different V family members in mammalian species. In addition, the diversity analysis is simplified because we are comparing mutation frequencies in a single FR across various genotypes and individual animals. Paired-end reads were assembled and preprocessed for length and V region open reading frame. Singleton sequences were eliminated, and sequences were translated into the predicted protein sequence. As shown in Figure 2a, 95% of the total sequence reads (n = 4.8x106 reads) of CmLC from the immunized birds contained 0–2 changes at the amino acid level, including 87% with no changes at all. In contrast, the normal OmniChicken light chain bulk repertoire contained only 0.8% sequences with 0–2 amino acid changes and 0.3% with no changes (n = 7.2 x106 reads from 6 birds). The mean number of light chain changes in OmniClic was 0.4 compared to 7.4 for OmniChickens. The frequencies of changes at the DNA level were similar: 94% vs. 0.6% for 0–2 changes in OmniChicken versus OmniClic. In contrast to the reduced levels of mutation in the light chains, heavy chains showed increased mutation levels in OmniClic compared to OmniChicken (Figure 2a). The mean number of changes in heavy chain was 13.3 in OmniClic, as compared to 11.5 in OmniChicken. The graphs in Figure 2a were calculated based on the number of changes in FR1 through FR3 and did not include CDR3, since there is no germline CDR3 sequence in the case of the rearranging heavy chain SynVH-SD that could be used to calculate the changes.

The frequency of unique CDR-H3s was strikingly higher in OmniClic heavy chains, indicating that more clonotypes were generated when the heavy chains were paired with CmLC1. This observation is consistent with the idea that the VH underwent enhanced selection for diverse sequences, not only in CDRs 1–2 as indicated in Figure 2a, but also in CDR3. To compare the results in Figure 2a using this type of analysis, the frequency of unique sequences was also calculated for the non-CDR3 portions of the V region (FR1 through FR3; Figure 2b right panel). OmniClic light chain had a much lower ratio of unique sequences than any of the other chains (Figure 2b), likely reflecting the fact that so many of the sequence reads were germline and would thus be counted as a single unique sequence. These results showed that there was no restriction in the B cell repertoire caused by the limitation of light chain diversity, but rather suggest that the lack of diversity in the light chains, and CDR3 in particular, leads to a compensatory increase in frequency of mutations in the heavy chain CDR3.

Even though the overall frequency of light chain mutations was much reduced in OmniClic, amino acid changes seemed to be clustered in the CDRs, suggesting that they were undergoing positive selection in the immune response (Fig. S5 shows plots of mutation by position in light chains). Interestingly, the amino acid diversity observed in the CDR-L3 NGS data appeared higher in OmniClic than in OmniChicken, as shown by the additional colors seen in the bars at CDR3 positions, even though the absolute frequency of these mutations was much lower in OmniClic. This result would indicate that some rare, mutated sequences were produced in OmniClic, and they were rarer than in OmniChicken.

### Identification of antigen-specific antibodies from OmniClic birds

To further characterize the antibodies that can be obtained from immunized OmniClic animals, mAbs were identified by single B cell screening, using gel-encapsulated microenvironment (GEM) technology.44 Antibodies were cloned in a single-chain variable fragment (scFv)-human Fc format. Two types of cloning strategies were pursued for antibodies from the OmniClic splenocytes. In one set of experiments, the native light chain sequence from the B cell was amplified and cloned with its paired VH, to capture and observe the frequency of mutations occurring in a cohort of antigen-specific antibodies produced in vivo. These experiments were done with one CmLC1/SynVH-C bird and one CmLC1/SynVH-SD bird. In other experiments, we amplified only the heavy chains from individual antigen-specific B cells and directly cloned them with the fully germline light chain. This direct cloning strategy with germline light chain would be the preferred route during an OmniClic antibody discovery campaign, as it would by definition produce only candidates with the desired attribute of working with the germline light chain. Cloning VH with the germline light chain is a more streamlined process requiring fewer amplification steps and is more efficient in the long run if one is only interested in heavy chains that can pair with the germline light chain. Any clones that require the mutations that might be present in their native light chains would drop out during the screening process, but our results show that we expect the number of such clones to be low.

In the first experiments, native light chains with their paired heavy chains were cloned. A cohort of 41 unique antibodies was obtained from 2 birds, and these were confirmed to bind PGRN by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Sequence analysis of the light chains showed that nearly one-fifth (4 of 16 for bird 45211 and 3 of 25 for bird 45331) of the light chains in these clones were fully germline in sequence (Figure 3a), and about 37% of the total had only 1 mutation. In the whole cohort, the median number of amino acid changes per V region was 1, and the average number of amino acid changes per clone was 2.4 (Figure 3a). These numbers are higher than in the bulk non-selected NGS data, indicating that selection for antigen binding enriched to a certain degree for mutated sequences, although much less than in regular OmniChickens (Figure 3a). The changes appear more likely to occur in the CDRs (Figure 3b), further indicating that they are functionally selected. The heavy chains in these antibodies showed levels of mutation similar to normal OmniChicken-derived antibodies to the PGRN target, unlike the increased mutation levels we observed in the NGS data.
